speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Miss Carney that Bill C-85, an Act to amend the Petroleum Incentives Program Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, in opening the debate for the Liberal Party I would like to comment on the address by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. McDermid). In his opening remarks he said that his Government was elected because the people wanted a change. I think they got it. A good Liberal Government has now been replaced by a Government which makes one devastatingly bad decision after another, which has a very detrimental effect on Canadians and their economic future.

The Parliamentary Secretary said it was a goal of the Government to do away with the National Energy Program. I would say that it was not only a goal, it was an obsession. Having developed this mania, the first and foremost pillar of the energy policy of this Government is to do away with anything that had any relationship whatsoever with the NEP. The Government did this instead of looking at the programs to determine for itself what would be in the best interests of Canadians.
Another thing of great concern to me is the abandonment of the Foreign Investment Review Agency and the implementation of Investment Canada. I am very concerned about this, particularly now. With the reduction of oil prices we are entering a period where Canadian companies with a high debt load are very, very vulnerable. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in his speech in New York in December of 1984 that Canada is open to investment. I am concerned that what Canada is open to is raids by foreign corporations on Canadian companies. If oil prices continue to decline and stay down, as I think they may, for even a short period of time, then Canadian companies with high debt loads and oil and gas reserves are very vulnerable to foreign multinationals who do not want to do their own exploration because they find it easier
and cheaper to pick up the assets of Canadian companies at bargain-basement prices. Nothing in this Government's philosophy would prohibit that from taking place. This situation has to be watched very closely because if we do not monitor it from the very beginning we could very much regret it later on.
The Parliamentary Secretary also mentioned that the Government was interested in the deregulation of communications. This also is a subject of great concern to me particularly where it affects the CBC which has had its budget severely reduced. The CBC is very much admired throughout the world, and for the last 40 years various Governments have considered it to be part of the cement that binds this country together. I am very concerned that it may be reduced to a remnant of its former self. I am also very concerned about our book publishing industry being placed on the table in our free trade negotiations with the United States. I am concerned as well about those negotiations themselves. The way this Government is developing it, free trade seems to boil down to: What does the United States want? Let us be nice to them. Let us be perceived as being more than friends, as being agreeable. Let us be perceived as not interfering with the wishes of the United States in whatever relationship it wishes to have with Canada. I think that is a rather frightening position to take, particularly when these free trade talks will have such tremendous importance for the future of Canada. If we tie ourselves down to a continental approach to free trade leaving no room for latitude on an international basis, and do away with the trade surplus that we have just because the United States is not happy with it, I think we will be asking for economic disaster in the future.
There is a position which could be taken which is more important and serves Canada's interests much better than does the present one. I am concerned that we are giving the country the appearance of being too agreeable. We are talking free trade with the United States in the belief that that is what they want to talk with us. The indications from Americans are not that they want to talk free trade on a one-on-one, equal-partner basis. We are having difficulty convincing the United States of the importance of some of our industries. I have already mentioned the book publishing industry and other things that we want to keep off the table. We are having trouble convincing them of the importance of our fisheries in Atlantic and western Canada and of the fact that these industries should not be available for countervailing tariffs.

I am replying to the comments made yesterday by the Parliamentary Secretary. If the Member will give me his continued attention, he will hear some other points which he may consider to be more relevant. I hope he will be generous in that regard.
I am also concerned about the attitude that is being taken in the United States with respect to the import of oil and gas, particularly that imported from Canada. As the Hon. Member who just intervened knows, as do all other Members in the House, the American Government wanted a more reasonable price for natural gas imported into the United States. This was granted and a very reasonable pricing mechanism was set in this regard. We are now hearing disturbing rumours of the possibility of an import tax to apply to oil and gas imported into the United States from Canada. This is all in the context of free trade and I think it is a disturbing environment in which to have these discussions on free trade.
I am also concerned about the comments of our chief negotiator who has mentioned that he favours the inclusion on the table of the sale of water from Canada to the United States. We know that eventually the thing that Americans will want most from Canada will be Canadian water. For the negotiator to say that what the Americans want most is what he wants to give them, does not appear to be good negotiating practice.
I feel that through this Bill the Government is abandoning the whole thrust of off-shore exploration. That is very damaging for frontier development. The Government has said that it is going to be doing away with the Petroleum Incentives Program, but will replace it with an exploration tax grant and that this will be the answer. However, that is certainly not the answer. We have seen that it is not the answer as exploration on all frontier areas, including the off-shore, is declining. It is maintaining a certain level that is not, in itself, alarming, mainly because the petroleum incentive grants will be continued until the end of March of this year and then will be grandfathered to December of 1987.
However, the outlook for the period after March 31 of this year, and particularly after December of 1987, is a concern to areas that have come to depend on off-shore explorations and to Canadians in general who are very concerned about the security of supply of oil and gas. That will be very, very important in the future. We cannot for a minute assume that our conventional resources will be enough to carry us through for very long. Due to the way in which we are selling them, we need to replenish our reserves in order to be able to assure Canadians that there are reserves within the Canadian boundaries that will be there when we need them.
It is shortsighted to ignore the security of supply question. I was pleased to hear the Parliamentary Secretary make mention of his Government's commitment to Canadianization. I do not, however, agree with his statistic that in the last year the Government increased Canadianization from 42 per cent to 47 per cent, more than the former Government did in the previous three years. In the previous three years the former Liberal Government increased Canadianization from 28 per cent to the 42 per cent level.
I am hoping that the Government will not rest on this statistic of 47 per cent, as the Parliamentary Secretary has assured me it will not. I hope the Government will continue to increase the Canadianization of our oil and gas industry. The increase from 42 per cent to 47 per cent is almost entirely the result of Olympia & York's purchase of Gulf Canada and the takeover of Gulf Canada's downstream assets by Petro-Canada in Ontario and western Canada. We now know, of course, that Ultramar has taken over the downstream assets of Gulf Canada in Quebec and Atlantic Canada.
It is very important that we maintain this Canadianization theme. That is not to exclude multinationals, because I feel that the exploration, refining, and marketing of oil and gas in the country owes a great deal to foreign corporations because they have shown us the way.
To a large extent, people who work for Canadian companies at present started in the oil and gas industry with multinational and foreign oil companies. However, we cannot forget about the Canadian aspect as, I think, has been done in this sale. 1 think we are telling Canadians that we will look at the statistics of Canadianization, but unless you are a Canadian company that can beef up the statistics and that is meaningful in the percentage of Canadianization, we really do not have time to be concerned about your problems. I am afraid that that will reflect itself if this new Bill is passed. This Bill is doing away with what was an 80 per cent grant under the Petroleum Incentives Program to Canadian companies that are not paying taxes and giving these same companies a 10 per cent grant, or 40 per cent of the exploration grants which the Government is offering under this proposed legislation.
I believe the effect of this will be to remove small Canadian companies completely from frontier exploration and place them in great difficulty. When one also considers the position in which the Government has placed Canadian companies as a result of the Western Accord, by not leaving any buffer for them in times of declining oil prices, one realizes that these Canadian companies will be hurt very badly.
It is unfortunate that the Government decided that it should remove the new oil reference price, which was of great help to Canadian companies. Now small Canadian companies that have investments and are indebted are on the same footing as the multinationals which have their resources and no debt problems. Furthermore, these multinationals have vast supplies of old oil on which they will be able to declare a windfall profit.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for protecting me from that unruly group opposite. Let me return to the very pertinent point I was making concerning Petro-Canada's very important role in developing the offshore exploration and delineating the reserves with respect to Hibernia. We have been encouraged in recent months by the finds in Hibernia, such as Ben Nevis. The most recent find is the Husky Bow Valley discovery. We have also been encouraged by the announced discovery by Gulf in the Beaufort. Therefore, we are finding very significant reserves of oil and gas on the frontiers. What is the policy of the Government with respect to utilizing and developing these discoveries in the near future? I suggest that it is as a result of the Petroleum Incentives Program that we have reserves that can be developed now.
I believe that a great deal more of delineation drilling must be carried out to establish further the size and context of these reserves. This will not happen under the amendment that the Government is making in Bill C-85, and I believe that is unfortunate.
At least through the actions of the former Government with the Petroleum Incentives Program we know that some reserves exist and can be developed in the near future. It is very important that these be developed soon because we are rapidly running out of conventional supplies, particularly in oil. If we do not begin planning to bring on these new supplies we will leave ourselves in a vulnerable position.
Let me explain the serious effects these provisions will have in Nova Scotia. In September, 1984, there were nine rigs operating off the coast of Nova Scotia. After the Government's announcement of these planned amendments to the Petroleum Incentives Program and its eventual replacement with the exploration grants, there was just one rig operating off the coast of Nova Scotia one year later. In September, 1984, there were 3,000 people employed in the offshore of Nova Scotia, but there are only 500 people employed at the present time. That is a very serious reduction in activity in

Nova Scotia and we hope that this can be turned around. However, in order for this to happen, it must be done by the multinationals through the format of these amendments.
The multinationals will wait until they feel the time is right to do any further work and, therefore, all of our frontier resources may be left where they are in their present undetermined and insufficient state of delineation. This is a concern to all of us who are worried about our security of supply, the Canadianization of our oil industry and the state of our energy policy in this country.
I believe it is significant to note that the Government has been saying continually that it wants the market to tell it exactly what should be done. I am afraid that the market will do just that, which means nothing will be done in the future in frontier development.
There is a severe contradiction in this case, which is typical of the Government. It relates to the specified portion which the Minister says she will invest between the end of March, 1986 and the grandfathering period for the Petroleum Incentives Program to the end of December, 1987, which allows the Minister to determine how much she will invest in the Petroleum Incentives Program. This gives her great latitude and directly contradicts her statement that she wanted to let the industry know what would be available to them so that everyone would have an equal opportunity.
There are those who say that all oil companies, regardless of their country of origin, should have an equal opportunity. I am not ashamed to say that this Party is not opposed to giving Canadian companies an advantage in this country. Canadian companies, particularly in the formative years, take very great risks because of the difficulty of establishing a foothold in the oil and gas sector. We have seen many of them suffer financial set-backs as a result of the recent recession. Some of them are still in difficulty, and I think it is unfortunate that these companies may not be allowed to regain their feet and participate in a meaningful way in this oil and gas exploration.
I ask the Government to reconsider these amendments and to consider proposals that have been made by other groups such as the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada who have set forth to the Minister their own recommendations for the replacement of or amendments to the Petroleum Incentives Program Act. Its recommendations were not adhered to. But if there should be changes to this program, then the changes presented by the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada are very reasonable and I think they should be examined and re-examined by the Government. I think it is unfortunate that that has not been done.
More consideration must be given to frontier development, to the areas affected and to our energy future. We must have assurance of supply. I am concerned that judging from the way the Government is talking, no special attention will be given to frontier oil exploration and development. I am not only concerned about the frontier but also about the fate of projects like the Husky upgrader. I feel as well that it is very important

to encourage exploration in the western sedimentary basin in western Canada. I think it is a very important sector for job creation and it will be very important for the economic development of western Canada. But the Government has given billions of dollars to the oil companies through the abandonment of the petroleum revenue gas tax. This will mean billions and billions of dollars lost to the private sector by 1990. One estimate is that by 1990 the Canadian taxpayer will have lost a total revenue source of $12.2 billion and this money will go to the oil and gas industry.
The Minister has said that she is confident that this will flow through to exploration and development, which will create an engine for growth in the energy sector and will be of benefit to all Canadians. We in the Liberal Party would like to be assured that this will happen, but we do not have confidence that either the Minister or this Government really know what they are doing in relation to this ambition. We have not seen any lasting indication other than some platitudes given out by the multinationals and the large players in the oil and gas industry. We have not seen any concrete action being taken. Granted, it will take time for the intentions of the industry to manifest themselves, but we have not seen the intention clearly that the industry, on a continuous basis, will put back into exploration and development what they have been given through the abandonment of the petroleum and gas revenue tax.
One of the great tests will be what this industry is going to do with respect to frontier development, if it is going to continue to explore. Indications are that it is moving away from frontier development. Fortunately, we have these optimistic finds which will, hopefully, keep the attention of the oil and gas sector so that it will continue to explore and develop these very great potentials. The tragedy is that it is almost certain that the small Canadian companies, and perhaps companies other than Petro-Canada, will not be able to participate in exploration and development when the PIP program is finally over.
I think it is very unfortunate for the long term future of our oil and gas industry that the Canadian companies are being shut out from the role they can play and the benefits they can achieve. I ask the Government to reconsider the amendments it is putting forward in Bill C-85. I ask it to consider the need for further exploration of the frontier and the fact that these resources should develop. I ask the Government to assure us that there will be a higher percentage of Canadian participation than is becoming evident at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, our energy critic is unavoidably absent today so I have the opportunity to say a few words about the Bill to amend the Petroleum Incentives Program Act. This was a controversial program right from the beginning. I remember it well when we were debating it during the debate on the series of Bills which brought in the National Energy Program. It was something that the New Democratic Party opposed at that time on the basis that this was another form of a historical series of giveaways to the energy sector and to the oil companies in
particular, and another form of the energy policy whereby Canadians should pay the shot for exploration, a policy entrenched over the years under successive Liberal Governments.
I believe at one time in the North we were paying 110 cents for every dollar that was spent on exploration. The Canadian taxpayer was taking all the risks, yet it was the companies which actually found some profit from the distribution and sale of that particular resource. So the Petroleum Incentives Program was part and parcel of that approach to energy development, and in that respect it deserved all the criticism it received at that time.
The irony is that that policy has been done away with by a Conservative Government, and one would like to think that is because there has been a change in direction. Well, there has been some change in direction in terms of the rhetoric of the Government about relying more on the market-place, but we still have an energy policy that is based on public risk and private development.
The Hon. Member who spoke before me indicated that the Government, although it is taking away the Petroleum Incentives Program from the energy companies, also gave to the oil companies in the form of the abolition of the PGRT some-to use the Hon. Member's figures-$12.2 billion. So we have not had a change in the over-all approach that the public should make the investment and take the risk, and the private sector, with the exception of Petro-Canada, should take the profit where profit is eventually made, in what I admit is sometimes a very long term process, with great lead times. Nevertheless it is a policy which we in the New Democratic Party find objectionable. We find it so because our view with respect to resource development has always been that if it is the public that has to pay for the exploration and the development and take the risk, then it is the public that should ultimately have the equity, ownership and control of those resources. This seems to me to be, in a strange way, in keeping with the free enterprise philosophy of Hon. Members opposite. Those people who take the risk ought to benefit when, having taken that risk, things turn out well. That has been the argument that has been preferred with respect to why entrepreneurs should have the full benefit of whatever profits come from their particular investment. After all, it was they who took the risk, so they should now reap the benefit, having been willing to take that risk with their money. I make the same argument on behalf of the Canadian public. If it is the money of the Canadian public which is being used to take the risk, if its money is being invested in exploration and development of energy resources, whether it is offshore, in western Canada or wherever it happens to be, it should be the public which reaps the benefit of that risk in terms of ownership, in terms of control and in terms of the ultimate profitability of the resource. For some reason or other that has always been an anathema to the Party which forms the Government now and, in many respects, it was only very partially accepted by the Liberal Party when it was in Government in the form of the National Energy Program.

Perhaps Governments have had to sink so much money in one way or another into oil and gas exploration because there is something fundamentally uneconomic about our approach to energy policy. I say "uneconomic", because if we use "economic" in the strict, capitalist sense of the word, and if exploration and development of these resources were so economic, it would not require massive public investment in the first place. This would have been something which the private sector could have done on its own in the expectation that it would have been a worth-while investment. I say that only to pose the question of whether or not we should have been on a different track altogether for some time now. Instead of our response to the fact of dwindling conventional oil reserves being that we had to search madly for every last drop of oil within our territory, regardless of the environmental and social consequences of that particular activity, we could have faced up to the fact that Joe Green was wrong in a different way. Joe Greene, the former Liberal Minister of Energy, told us at one time that we had enough conventional oil to last us for hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of years. That was just before the energy crisis.
We could have faced up to the fact that Joe Greene was wrong by taking a conservationist approach to energy policy. I realize that some things happened. There was the Canadian Home Insulation Program and the program for conversion from oil to gas. There has been a number of conservation programs undertaken by various levels of Government in Canada. However, all these things together are just a drop in the bucket compared with the money which the public has been consistently asked to spend on this other approach, that is, to spend billions and billions and billions of dollars on frontier oil and gas exploration.
I am not maintaining that these resources should never be developed, but I am maintaining that they should be developed by the public, for the public and only when it is possible to do it in a way which does not disrupt the very sensitive environment or ecosphere that we find, for instance, in Arctic Canada. The price we will pay to find that last barrel of oil, if we go about it in the way in which we are now going, will be too high in the final analysis, not just in terms of price per barrel on the market-place or what we may not get back for our investment, but too high in terms of the social and ecological consequences.
1 think also of what could be the consequences of too rapid or too eager development of our offshore resources in Atlantic Canada. Perhaps people who are on site and are involved in it have less reason to worry than someone, 1 admit, speaking from a distance who has not been able to see exactly what is happening. However, I say this as one who worries about these things. It has been one of my nightmares that there should be a blow-out on the East Coast and that terrible damage should be done to our fishery, a renewable resource which, if cared for properly, could go on for thousands and thousands and thousands of years. Yet, we put these renewable and everlasting resources at risk when we try to do things in a hurry because we are not willing to take another and possibly even more
Petroleum Incentives Program Act difficult approach in terms of public opinion, that is, to ask Canadians to accept the reorganization of our energy life so that we can be more conserving of the resources that we have and do not have to be pushed to the wall in the development of as yet unavailable resources. I put before the House this choice, which I think we still have not in the expectation that the Government will suddenly change its mind, but because I think these things have to be put on the record constantly.
In this context, because I have been talking about our whole approach to energy policy and because the Bill is part and parcel of the Government's approach to energy policy, I should like to say a word about the role which I think Petro-Canada could play in our energy policy, if the money, for instance, which was being saved by the cancellation of this particular program were to be used for the appropriate expansion and development of Petro-Canada. I find it increasingly difficult these days to speak about Petro-Canada because not only the Conservative Government but the Liberal Government before it asked Petro-Canada to operate in a way quite similar to any other large corporation. For me, this violates the reason we want a Crown corporation in the first place. Crown corporations have been put in a very difficult position because they have been asked by successive Governments to operate on a commercial basis, going back to the mid-1970s when the Government of that day asked the CNR to operate strictly on a commercial basis. It has not as yet totally done that, but it has made decisions on that basis. Crown corporations by these decisions have been put in a very difficult position. They have been unable to operate in a way that would bring to them the kind of credit which could and would come to a Crown corporation if it were to do what my colleagues and I think Crown corporations should do in any event, that is, to be an actor in the market-place, which is different from the role of other actors in the market-place. Petro-Canada, unlike other Crown corporations, should be an example to others in northern development when it comes to dealing with native people and to a sensitivity to the environment. It should be an example when it comes to sensitivity to employment needs and the needs of communities, workplace safety and health, all these kinds of things. However, I have to report sadly that this is not the case. There has been the odd occasion when Petro-Canada has done something which was a cut above the rest of them, but on many other things I have been furious with Petro-Canada for acting just like every other corporation.

Petro-Canada has, like everyone else, done away with its full service stations and the jobs that are available to young people. They tore out their full service stations and put up self-serve stations. In my view we have far too many of them. I would have thought that PetroCan, of all Crown corporations, would not have done that, or that it would not have been a Crown corporation that tore up a very traditional location in Winnipeg of a restaurant and gas station and put in a self-serve station.
These actions, as well as those with regard to price, have, over the years, eroded to a certain extent the enthusiasm that

January 28, 1986
Petroleum Incentives Program Act people have had for PetroCan. I want to say to the House, and to Canadians through the House: Do not be discouraged about the possibilities because of what various Crown corporations have been instructed to do by their various Governments. The Crown corporations still have that potential, which was always there and stil is there, to be the kind of economic instrument that the people who originally thought of Crown corporations knew they could be, that is, acting in the public interest and able to do things that other corporations are not able to do, and do them better, in a more socially and ecologically responsible way because they are backed up by the Government and by the people of Canada through their Government. They do not have to be accountable to their short-term profit margins.They do not have to make bad decisions based on what their last quarterly profit margin was. They do not have to lay off people to get a better credit rating because, as it is now, the Government has said to them, "You have to borrow money on the open market now; you cannot come to us any more".
All these bad decisions that Crown corporations make often have their origin in the instructions that they have been given by Governments. That is why these are fundamentally political questions in the final analysis. People are angry. I have complaints about PetroCan not charging less for gas than other companies. Well, it is very difficult for a Crown corporation to operate that way if it has been told by Government that that is not the way it is supposed to operate. In some cases the people like to have it both ways. They want Crown corporations to make money, they do not want them to lose money, but at the same time they want the Crown corporations to give them a break in terms of price. There is that irony there as well.
In any event, I think the larger point is that the relationship between how we understand Crown corporations, how Governments understand them, and the instructions that are given to them. Also, how they behave in the market-place has to be better understood than it is now. Instead what we have from this Government is a mysterious policy. We are not sure whether it is asking PetroCan to behave in certain ways because it is setting it up for privatization. We are not sure exactly what the Government is doing, as is the case with so many other things that the Government does, because there are mixed messages. I suppose only time will tell just exactly what sinister plots lurk in the minds of those who will make the final decisions with respect to the future of PetroCan.
I say to the Government that if it thinks the imagination of Canadians has in any way been diminished over the last several years about what is possible in terms of public ownership in this country in those very, very important sectors of our economy like energy, then it is very sadly mistaken. That imagination may have been dulled somewhat over the years by the bad name that has been given to public ownership by successive Liberal Governments. It is still there and any Government that moves to extinguish it by making a move on PetroCan or any other major Crown corporation in this country will find, to its lamentable surprise, that the Canadian people will not put up with that kind of action.
What we have before us is a very minor amendment. It is not minor in terms of money, but it is minor in terms of changes of approach. To my mind, the Conservative and Liberal approaches to energy development, to my mind, have more similarities than they have differences. It is in the interests of both the Liberal and the Conservative Parties to make out as if they had very serious differences about how energy should be developed in this country. It serves to distract people from the fact that there are a great many more similarities than differences. The more fundamental thing to say is that the approach of both this Government and of its predecessor Government has been very, very similar. I think the extent to which it is different is the extent to which this Government at least says that it wants to rely more on the market-place. It may find that the market-place is not the happy, productive, fruitful context that it maintains it is. When it does that, maybe Canadians will then be at a point once again when they can reconsider their energy future and ask for a Government that would opt for an energy future that is based on conservation and on development of renewable resources, and that is based on a picture of the future that does not just extend into the next decade or into the decade after that, but one which tries to carry out what could be called responsible stewardship, not just for the near future but also for the future that belongs to generations to come.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raised the point of the statutory nature of PetroCan. The point we have been trying to make in the last few days is the one that the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) tried to make yesterday in response to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) who was reading to the House what she called the mandate of PetroCan. It was not so much the mandate of PetroCan but what she had instructed PetroCan to do and how she had instructed it to act as of a certain date.
The fact is that the mandate for PetroCan is in the legislation. If the Government wants to change the mandate of PetroCan, it ought not to do that simply by issuing instructions from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Government should return to the House of Commons to change the mandate of PetroCan. That is certainly in keeping with the kinds of things I know Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament have said over the years about Parliament being involved in instructions to Crown corporations so that things do not happen by ministerial decree over and above what Parliament had already decided. The point we have been trying to make these last few days is that if the mandate of PetroCan is to be changed, let it be changed here in the House of Commons and not by ministerial decree.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak this morning in support of Bill C-85, an Act to amend the Petroleum Incentives Program Act. There were three demand-driven programs of the National Energy Program that created uncertainties in estimating and containing costs in the National Energy Program expenditures. They were, the Canadian Home Insulation Program, the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and the Petroleum Incentives Program grants. We have disposed of two of those, and now Bill C-85 disposes of the final one, one which an oil analyst has called a bad dream.
This nation's energy riches should no longer be a source of endless division and regional tension, the results of the National Energy Program. The NEP was not in any sense a national program and was only indirectly an energy program. Its central and urgent goal was to implement a political and regional program designed to keep the Liberal Party in power through the strengthening of that Party's appeal to the voters and/or consumers of central Canada.
During the years between 1973 and 1984, the producing provinces and companies had been required to subsidize directly the central Government and consumers through artificially low prices for crude oil and natural gas to a cumulative total of over $50 billion. The provisions of the National Energy Program, therefore, only further compounded the antagonism of the producing provinces which were suffering the consequences of this unfair treatment. The program was conceived under a
Petroleum Incentives Program Act veil of secrecy, designed to victimize a region and an industry without any discussion with the concerned provinces or the industry.
Three stated objectives of the NEP were, increased Canadian content in the energy industry, oil self-sufficiency by 1990, and increased fairness in revenue sharing. In reality, the publicly stated objectives, each sounding sincere and reasonable, were simply smokescreens for the true but hidden objectives of the program which were more wealth and more power for Ottawa. The Western Accord put a stop to the most vicious raid on the resources of one region to the principal benefit of another region that had occurred in the history of the country.
There can be no doubt that the two big losers as a result of this program have been the consumers and the Canadian exploration firms. Officials in Ottawa decided that they knew better than the market where exploration dollars should be directed. The infamous PIP system, biased in favour of Canadian firms, seduced many of them into unfamiliar and financially dangerous operations. Normal exploration investment criteria were discarded because 80 per cent of the funds came on request from Ottawa.
What has been achieved? No new major fields have been discovered. What has been lost? A great deal has been lost. Billions of precious exploration dollars have been misdirected and we have lost that greatest of all assets in the energy business, time. Investment decisions have been distorted and the future of a number of Canadian firms was placed at a very great risk. The authors of the National Energy Program failed to understand the basic reality of resource investment, which is the law of supply and demand. Even OPEC is now realizing that it cannot escape this discipline for very long.
A few years back, world prices would have resulted in a much larger piece of the revenue pie for Canada. Canadians working amicably together have never failed to make arrangements that serve the nation, and I am proud to say Albertans have always been major players in the attainment of these national purposes. Other countries adjusted more quickly to the real world of energy costs than Canada because of Liberal consumer-shielding policies. As a result, we lost ground in the competitive industrial markets of the world. The price freeze of 1973 was the industry's sentence, and its guillotine was the National Energy Program.
PIP grants were intended to meet not only the Canadianiza-tion and the 1990 self-sufficiency goals but also the need to know goal. Significant savings in PIP expenditures were achieved through the commitment by Alberta to the market development incentive program through which Alberta virtually took over the PIP program in the province itself. PIP was called a lot of things including a massive misdirection of taxpayers' money and a program that actually encouraged companies to drill dry holes.
When in opposition, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) asked the then Minister if there were some limits to the hand-outs he was prepared to give to the oil and gas companies. The Auditor General pointed out in his 1983 Report that performance measurement systems,

January 28, 1986
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
although more advanced in the PIP operations, were generally not well developed for evaluating efficiency and developing and making comparisons to the standards. Although an attempt to develop a framework for monitoring the program's impact and effect was undertaken at one point, it was actually never pursued and it cost the federal Treasury an average of $1.6 billion per year, money that was subsidizing activity rather than rewarding success.
This Bill eliminates PIP incentives as of March 31, 1986. From that day forward companies wishing to explore and develop Canada's oil and gas resources will have to do so on the basis of geological and economic factors, not on the basis of Government hand-outs.
We are not abandoning previous commitments. PIP commitments which were in place before the announcement of the Western Accord will be honoured until the end of 1987. This generous grandfathering provision will enable industry to adjust to the new approach. That approach puts the emphasis on opportunities created in the market-place. Politicians and bureaucrats will no longer determine where the industry should be drilling for oil and gas. Once again, those decisions will be in the hands of industry.
The Government of Canada recognizes frontier exploration as a high risk investment which requires additional incentives to help bridge the gap between the termination of PIP and the timing of expected frontier oil and gas developments. Recently, we announced that a new tax base incentive will be introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). This 25 per cent exploration tax credit will be applicable to exploration expenses in excess of $5 million per well for wells drilled anywhere in Canada. To ensure that the credit assists companies which are currently non-tax paying, it will be refundable at a rate of 40 per cent.
The exploration tax credit was made available beginning December 1 and will terminate December 31, 1990. It is an equitable and cost effective measure to encourage frontier exploration without discriminating against other regions. We anticipate the tax credit will cost taxpayers between $150 million and $250 million annually. PIP cost us some $1.6 billion annually.
In replacing PIP with a tax-base incentive we have fulfilled one of the specific commitments made in the Prince Albert statement of July, 1984. Hon. Members are well aware of the Prince Albert statement. It was a key element in the election platform on which the Progressive Conservative Party won the most resounding electoral victory in the country's history. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has said, we have achieved virtually all the goals we set for ourselves at Prince Alberta. We promised to use energy as an engine of growth, and we have done so. We promised increased Canadian participation in the energy industry, and we have achieved it. We promised fair treatment of consumers and producers; both groups are now benefiting from our policies. We promised co-operation between the federal and provincial Governments and industry, and we have delivered upon that promise as well. The Atlantic and Western Accords, the new frontier energy policy, and the natural gas markets and pricing agreement are proof that the Prince Albert statement was, in fact, a constructive reaction to the previous Government's destructive National Energy Program. In March we signed the Western Accord with the Provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The agreement radically restructured the operating environment for the energy industry in Canada.
The previous Government was fond of acronyms. We eliminated a long list of them in the Western Accord, ones such as COSC, Canadian ownership special charge; PCC, petroleum compensation charge; and the IORT, the incremental oil revenue tax. They were representative of the burdensome tax regime under which the petroleum industry had been labouring.
As a result of the Western Accord, oil exploration in western Canada is now higher than at any time in our history. The number of wells drilled is up 23 per cent over the the comparable pre-Accord period. Land sales are up an amazing 73 per cent, which means there will be even more exploration in the West next year. The benefits from exploration and production activity do not stop at the Manitoba border. Investment and employment spinoffs will stimulate economic activity in all regions of the country. We are replacing a rigid frontier royalty regime with one that is flexible and profit-sensitive.
The National Energy Program enabled the Government to confiscate 25 per cent of successful oil and gas development in the frontier. This Government does not confiscate property. There will be no Crown share provision in the new regime. Our commitment to 50 per cent Canadianization ownership on frontier production projects is as strong as that of our predecessors; but we will achieve this goal in a more equitable and more realistic fashion.
In summary, our frontier energy policy establishes a profit-sensitive royalty regime. It establishes non-discriminatory and regionally balanced exploration incentives and a stable management regime. Finally, it establishes fair Canadianization requirements.
Oil and gas investment intentions are up by about $2 billion-more than 25 per cent over last year. This investment is creating thousands of new jobs right across the country by stimulating the exploration activity which contributes to our energy security. Foreign investors are looking favourably on Canada once again. Salomon Brothers of New York recently published a ringing endorsement of our new energy policy and investment climate. Canada can benefit from increased foreign investment. Without it, many of our energy projects simply would not proceed. No foreign investment would mean lost opportunities, lost jobs and reduced energy security.
The overhaul of the National Energy Program was one of the five economic initiatives identified by the Progressive Conservatives when we were elected last year. The others were: reduction of the deficit, establishment of a positive investment climate, strengthening of Canada's trade relations, and removal of Government obstacles in the market-place.
January 28, 1986

Important advancements have been made in each of these areas. We reduced spending this year by $4.4 billion and we have identified cuts of some $75 billion from planned expenditures by 1990. The restrictive Foreign Investment Review Agency was replaced by Investment Canada, a body which actively solicits foreign investment. We have initiated discussions on a new trade agreement with the United States. This agreement is vital to our future economic growth. The Pacific Rim has also been identified as a priority area for trade development. We removed Government obstacles in the market-place, not only in the energy industry but in other key sectors such as transportation and communication.
In the second quarter our energy trade balance of payments rose by approximately $400 million over the same period last year. Business investment was up by an annual rate of 11 per cent in the third quarter of 1985. Residential housing investment, an excellent indicator of consumer confidence, rose 63 per cent in the third quarter, one of the largest increases in ten years.
The people of Canada elected the Progressive Conservatives on the basis of our campaign promises. What sets us apart from the previous Government is that we have delivered on those promises in the energy sector, and in other sectors. That is why this country is back on the road to economic recovery.
It has been a pleasure for me to speak in support of Bill C-85 this morning.

speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member on her speech and the defence she made not only of her Party's policies but of the region she comes from. She said that under the National Energy Program more wealth and power came to Ottawa. The corollary, of course, is that there was less wealth and power in the West. Would she also not agree that a case may be made that wealth and influence was distributed a little more across the country? Would she not agree that because of the NEP we had more drilling offshore? Husky, which is I think threatened under this new policy, was a major player in the Newfoundland offshore. Canadian companies benefited. Canadians got jobs in areas where unemployment is the highest in the country. This would not have happened if the NEP was not in place. She is right when she says more wealth came from the West to Ottawa, but to be fair, would she not agree that wealth was distributed to the Atlantic, jobs were distributed to the Atlantic, and Canadian companies participated in exploration in the Atlantic offshore which would not have been able to do so otherwise?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's questions. I would like to address them first in the context of the PGRT which was implemented under the NEP in 19801981. The PGRT was a tax on gross revenues at the well-head and could not be deducted for purposes of corporate taxes. In effect it was double taxation. This unfair taxation forced many
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
of our resource companies to cut back on their exploration budgets. If not half, easily 38 per cent of the drilling rigs in western Canada were forced to move out of the country or else the companies involved simply went broke. It also created extremely high unemployment in western Canada. Alberta's rate of unemployment went up from 3 per cent to 13 per cent to 13.5 per cent, and that is a huge jump. I recognize eastern Canada's problems, but you cannot compare them because we went up from 3 per cent to 13.5 per cent, and that is an increase of more than 450 per cent. All these people out of work meant increased unemployment insurance payments as well as welfare benefits. It was a tremendous burden on our social programs.
My hon. colleague knows that most of the money raised through the PGRT was used to offset the PIP grants. That was extremely costly. It was also discriminatory because the Liberal Government was saying that if you drill in a certain area we are going to supply 80 cents or 90 cents on the dollar. Without good, sound business judgment and good geological surveys, companies were forced into the frontiers and there is very strong evidence to indicate that they drilled dry holes simply for the sake of getting money.
You do not have to be a politician to know that you should spend your dollars wisely. The program we have introduced of gradually reducing the PIP grants and bringing in a 25 per cent tax credit incentive, is going to put the resource companies in a position where they base their drilling programs on good geological surveys and good seismic tapes before they start drilling exploratory wells. We are creating a climate which is far more beneficial for all firms.
I recognize that drilling activity on the East Coast was very strong over the last few years and the companies involved certainly were using the PIP grants. However, a lot of the activity was in areas where they did not have good geological information. I hope that over the next few years the proven reserves in the Venture situation will produce more proven reserves and that we can get some production, because certainly New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, that whole area, needs the jobs. I have to agree with the Hon. Member there. However, I think it was unfair for the Government to be handing out taxpayers' dollars to influence people to drill anywhere they wanted just so they could get tax dollars. The PGRT did put more money into Ottawa's hands and created a lot of animosity out West. The Government did not really consult or communicate with the provinces or the industry. It is most important and to everyone's benefit that we communicate and talk about our concerns and problems, not just the Government and the industry but consumers are winners as well.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member also said that there should be fair treatment for producers and consumers. Is it fair to say, in doing away with the PGRT and the increase in federal taxes on gasoline, that perhaps the burden of taxation has been shifted from producers to consumers? Are consumers, particularly motorists, not paying now a greater share? We just learned a few days ago that the major oil companies' profits have increased greatly over the last year.

January 28, 1986
Petroleum Incentives Program Act yet they are paying less, as my hon. friend has just pointed out, because they are not paying the PGRT. Consumers have seen federal taxes on gasoline go up 58 per cent in one year. I agree with the Hon. Member that there must be fair treatment of producers and consumers right across the country. However, would she agree that there has been some shifting of taxation from producers to consumers?

No, I cannot agree with my hon. colleague from Newfoundland. The phasing out of the PGRT is, in one respect, putting more money back into the ground to allow further exploration and development in the resource area. If we allow resource companies the flexibility to invest in Canada, and their investment is up $2 billion over the last year, they will create jobs. People will get off of unemployment insurance and welfare. These jobs are created not just in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. A lot of people from eastern Canada live in Alberta, especially Fort McMurray.
Yes, eight thousand.

Eight thousand. I am thrilled about that because this country has to work together. That is what the Hon. Member is driving at. We have to look at all regions and their economies. I cannot agree that it has shifted the tax burden. It does allow resource companies the flexibility to go out and invest in the country, create more activity and jobs. We will then have more housing starts and get people off social welfare programs.
The new 25 per cent tax credit will work extremely well. The Government has discussed this with the industry and its provincial counterparts. They have all agreed. So I am sorry but I cannot agree with the Hon. Member concerning the shifting of the burden.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a brief comment on the exchange between the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) and the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mrs. Sparrow). They have talked about some programs and creating employment in one region or another. We should remember that we do not make good use of our resources and make our country strong by weakening one region as compared to another. There may be concern about jobs that were created in the eastern part of the country as a result of the National Energy Program remaining, but he should remember what the National Energy Program did to western Canada. I have never heard a more graphic illustration of what the National Energy Program meant to western Canada than this: I had an opportunity to talk to a young couple in northern Alberta who were in the energy business. They were digging sump pits and preparing sites for drilling rigs. They were a young couple, presumably in their mid-thirties, starting out with a stake in their country, building a home in a community, and establishing some family ties and roots. They told me that when the National Energy Program came out they went to work the next morning digging sump pits. As a result of the National Energy Program's impact on the
company they were working for, they filled in those same holes that afternoon.
That is what the National Energy Program did to western Canadian drilling activity, and that affected jobs right across the country. We should bear in mind that if we have a resource, it is Canadian and should be thought about as being developed in the Canadian context for the good of all Canadians rather than for the sake of pitting one region against the other.
When one thinks in terms of what happened to the one young couple whom I had an opportunity to visit with in northern Alberta, and of how that related to the whole province and the whole western region, one has an idea of the impact on employment in that part of the country and what it subsequently did to employment in other parts of the country. We should think about this as a natural resource for the benefit of all Canadians, rather than talking about whether one region should have it or someone else should control it. We should develop it in the best interests of us all.

Mr. Speaker, the value of this Parliament was brought home to me again today because, following my friend from Calgary South, I get the opportunity to give a view from the Atlantic region. I thought her speech was a good one and that she certainly defended her particular area, which is what she was sent here to do. She certainly defended the policies of her Party, which is also what she was sent here to do. However, it is for the people of Canada to judge. I think that in any fair debate there must be a balance in order to let them come to that judgment. I would like to try to give a view from Atlantic Canada because its view of PIP and the National Energy Program is quite different.
The Hon. Minister across the way says that it is a Canadian resource which must be treated as such and looked at fairly. It is true that it is a Canadian resource. The problem is that that Canadian resource is in various parts of the country. It is in the West, in the East, and in the Beaufort. We are not talking about weakening one area at the expense of the other, but about the regional disparity that exists in the country. All sections of the country are not equal.
There are 8,000 people from the Atlantic area in Fort MacMurray simply because there are no jobs back home for them to take. I do not think it is a bad thing for Atlantic Canadians to be working in the West. Thank God that the West was able to produce jobs when it did. However, a lot of those people would rather have stayed at home if they could have done so. The greatest export of Atlantic Canada has been some of our best young people. It is not that they do not like western Canada. They have simply had to go there because they had no alternatives. I would rather they had chosen western Canada as an alternative, given options, rather than simply have gone there because they had to. That is the problem in the Atlantic area.
January 28, 1986

I hope that sets the theme for what I want to say. I am talking about an area which, historically in the country since Confederation, has been disadvantaged. We do not like that, but it is a reality. That is the basis upon which I want to make my remarks, Mr. Speaker.
As 1 see it, the scrapping of PIP means a reduction of activity in the off-shore in the Atlantic. That is, indeed, borne out by statements from some people in the oil industry. The Canadian Petroleum Association says it is a step forward for the energy policy in the country. Mr. Jim Hamilton, an oil industry analyst in Calgary, says that the bottom line is that there will be greater activity in the western sedimentary basin. That is our fear. We know what the track record is. We know that under PIP there was activity off-shore. We know that under PIP there were drill rigs out there. We know that under PIP more Newfoundlanders got jobs on the off-shore than ever before. Eighty of them lost their lives on the Ocean Ranger, but more of then went back after the Ocean Ranger sank because they wanted jobs and they wanted to make their contribution in developing the off-shore of Canada.
That activity existed under PIP. We do not know whether it would have existed had PIP not been there because it was there and it did the job. Not only did it put Canadian drill rigs there, it required that every company that wanted to drill off-shore must show a percentage of Canadian materials used and a percentage of Canadians employed in order to get those grants. The grants were not simply to drill. There were strings attached which were peculiarly Canadian. That is what I am afraid will now stop.
I also think the preference for Canadian companies is a concern for oil associations in the Atlantic area. The Association of Atlantic Petroleum Producers is concerned about this very fact as well. In an area where unemployment is the highest in Canada, we see the danger of the reduction of the kind of activity that has given us jobs. The fact is that jobs are now reduced from 3,000 in the Atlantic off-shore in 1984 to about 500.
This is what the Conservative Government has been putting forward as the fundamental plank in its platform. Whenever we ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) a question, she says that the Government has signed the Western Accord and the Atlantic Accord and that they are the cornerstone of its economic and job-creation policy for the Atlantic region and for Newfoundland. I am concerned about that from the point of view of exploration activity and further proving of the reserves that are there.
We have complained about the cut-backs in Government programs such as RRAP, CHIP, and COSP, which my hon. friend referred to. It is true that they have cut back CHIP and COSP, which existed not only for conservation and off-oil purposes, but were also creating a lot of jobs for small businesses. The carpenters, electricians, plumbers, pipefitters, and people who install tiles and insulation, were all working with small businesses. The incentive to do that no longer exists and a lot of small businesses have dried up.
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
However, when we complain about the cut-backs in such programs, about lay-offs in the Ministry of Transport and the Department of Fisheries, and about the possible closing down of railways and two heavy water plants in the Atlantic area, the Minister of Energy says that oil is going to be the saviour, that the day is coming when oil will create those jobs in the Atlantic area. When we complain about reductions in social security, about changes in the Unemployment Insurance Program, and about changes in family allowances and the old age pension, they still tell us to wait, that oil is going to be the engine of the economy in Atlantic Canada. They say that oil is going to create those jobs and that people with those jobs are going to pay the taxes which will look after family allowances, old age pensions, and unemployment insurance. Well, is it, Mr. Speaker? We have seen no evidence that that is the case so far.
The fundamental assumption of the Conservative Party is that we must let the private sector do the job and leave business alone. PIP was the direct opposite. It was government intervention to encourage and coax the private sector into exploring in areas where it was not before, into using Canadian materials, and into creating jobs in an area of Canada that was desperate for employment. That was the role of the Petroleum Incentives Program. It was Government intervention in the private sector in order to skew, bias and focus that private sector on an area that needed that attention. Where is the incentive for the private sector to continue that exploration offshore now that the world oil price is dropping?
We fear, as Mr. Hamilton said, that the bottom line is that there will be greater activity in the western sedimentary basin.
I am not attempting to pit one section against the other because I think it is wrong in this country, as my hon. friend has said, that one region should prosper at the expense of another. I simply want to state the case in the area from which I come.
We have been assured that Hibernia is still on target in spite of the fact that the world price is going down. We also know that the Offshore Trade Association of Nova Scotia has pleaded with the Government for special measures for the East Coast. It has said that there must be special measures for the East Coast in view of what the Tory Party has announced. The Offshore Trade Association of Nova Scotia-not the Liberal Party, the New Democratic Party or consumers-said that the new policy will kill exploration off Atlantic Canada. I am a layman and I must take the word of the private sector in Atlantic Canada. It says that this new policy will kill exploration in Atlantic Canada.
The Independent Petroleum Association also wants change. Under the new plan, non-taxable Canadian companies will recoup only 10 per cent of costs, whereas under the National Energy Program it would have been 80 per cent to 90 per cent. I must mention Husky Oil again among these many small Canadian companies because Bob Blair has been a major player in the offshore of the Atlantic. I congratulate him as a

January 28, 1986
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
Canadian for the role he has played. I hope he continues the work he has been doing because we need people like him.
We need him in the offshore, but whereas he received 80 per cent or 90 per cent before, he will only get 10 per cent now. Perhaps his company will become non-taxable, but my fear is that those changes which will take place will not be of benefit in the Atlantic area. I fear that many small Canadian companies will not be involved in frontier exploration. Even the Canadian Petroleum Association agrees that there will be less activity in the Atlantic and more activity in the western sedimentary basin.
Many in Atlantic Canada believe that the tendency is for the Government no longer to look after our interests. What is the evidence to support that view?
First, there are the cut-backs in Government programs on which we have historically depended. The Provinces of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have been at a disadvantage since they joined Confederation. We lost our traditional trading markets and became a colony of central Canada. Newfoundland was a colony of Britain and we transferred our colonial status from Britain to central Canada. This was not done through any devious means by any Party, but it is simply a reality.
We must recognize that there are disadvantaged areas that need special help. However, that special help through Government support, intervention and assistance has been dropping. The Atlantic area has historically depended on Government programs, but those government programs have been slashed. Naturally, we are hardest hit because when central Canada catches a cold we get pneumonia. That is the reality in this country.
We have been thrown to the private sector, but the private sector in Atlantic Canada is historically weak. We do not have manufacturing. We are a natural resource based economy which exports fish, lumber, pulp and paper, minerals and young people. We do not produce automobiles or manufactured goods. We do not produce value-added foodstuffs. The private sector in the Atlantic provinces has been historically weak, and we are told that companies outside the Atlantic provinces which have been in their present locations for a number of years are heading to the West.
We have seen world prices plummet under the present Government, yet there is no Government policy to protect Canadian consumers. However, there was a made-in-Canada price under the National Energy Program. Now we are at the mercy of the war between OPEC and the North Sea. When the Minister is asked why the multinationals are still making huge profits in light of falling prices, she states that it is necessary to do so in order to carry out exploration and drilling. Yet we are told by the Canadian Petroleum Association and the offshore industry in Atlantic Canada that these activities are moving to the West and there must be special arrangements made for the Atlantic area. How will the Minister focus that exploration and drilling on the offshore?
The Minister says that the high federal taxes on gas are necessary in order to pay for social programs. If that is true, why is the Government cutting unemployment insurance and family allowance? Why is it cutting out programs such as COSP, CHIP and RRAP? Why is the Government laying off civil servants in Fisheries and Transport? The Government is fundamentally affecting the economy of the Atlantic area as a result of such action.
I suggest that PIP is a graphic illustration that we are the victims of a double-whammy in the Atlantic region. Government services, including social security, are being cut back, yet incentives to the private sector are being taken away. There is no focusing of the private sector in that area and, whether or not the Government realizes it, it has cut the Atlantic adrift by its non-interventionist attitude toward the private sector. 1 submit that that is the issue as we debate the Petroleum Incentives Program.
That program graphically illustrates the difference between the policies of the previous Government and the present Government. We knew that we had to give special help to the Atlantic area because of its unique situation. We also knew that that area would be lost without the help of the federal Government. However, the Tories have said that they are withdrawing in order to make room for the private sector which will benefit that area. Where is the evidence of that? The same article from which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) quoted that 400,000 new jobs have been created indicated that 8 per cent of those new jobs are in the Atlantic area. While I welcome the fact that there are more jobs in Quebec and Ontario, which is good for Canada, my point is that every federal Government in this country must have a regional development policy. All areas of this country are not equal. While I do not want to set one area against another or see division in this country, I do want fairness and equity. I do not see any evidence of that in this new program. I believe that cut-backs in the Petroleum Incentives Program and the PGRT are symptomatic of the Government's new approach.
We saw the same thing in the late 1950s and early 1960s when Mr. Diefenbaker was Prime Minister. He attempted to do away with a section of the Terms of Union called Term 29 which allowed us equalization payments over a period of time in view of the disadvantage we suffered. People wore black arm bands in Newfoundland as a result of that, and it is pretty close to the time when we have to trot them out again. Quite seriously, if there is not a change or a recognition that there are stronger and weaker sections of the country, particularly within the private sector, if there is no recognition of regional disparity and some attempt to come to grips with it and to devise policy to overcome the problem, then we are not going to have a strong country.
We do not want to be a have-not area. We want to make our contribution. I referred earlier to the 80 people who lost their lives on the Ocean Ranger. Even after that rig sank, young Newfoundlanders went back to the rigs on the offshore with all
January 28, 1986

the dangers attached to them because they wanted to make a contribution not just to themselves, their families and their province, but to this country. What they are asking for is an opportunity to do that.
I say to the Government that it is not going to make that happen by doing away with Government intervention in the economy. This Government, like previous Governments, has to support and protect the livelihood of the people who work and live in the Atlantic area.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). I certainly agree that eastern Canada does have some problems. I agree with him that we should not pit one region against the other. However, on September 4, 1984, the Conservative Government came into power and faced a massive national debt of some $200 billion. It costs us and the people of Canada $26 billion per year just to service the debt which was left to us by the previous Government. If we do not address this situation-and I want to add that the Government is addressing the situation-we will end up in a disastrous state. For every $3 we raise in revenue, $1 goes to service the debt. If we do not attack this national debt today, in five years it will take $2 out of $3, and we will have to cut down on at least a third, if not 50 per cent, of all of our social programs. So we are taking a look at absolutely every area, every portfolio, and we are simply looking at it from the perspective of the national debt.
The Hon. Member said something about closing the heavy water plants in the East. Was it New Brunswick?
Nova Scotia.

Nova Scotia. I am the Chairman of the National Resource Committee. We have had the AECL appear before us and, if I understand my facts, those two heavy water plants had a 12-year supply but there was no market for their commodity. This does not make economic sense. Actually, in all reality, these plants should have been cut back and terminated many, many years ago.
I also wanted to ask my colleague about Canadian exploration and development expense. The Government has in place two expenses. With respect to the tax breaks which are being given, possibly the Hon. Member is closer to that than I am, but 1 understand that small Canadian companies which before could take advantage of the PIP program may not be able to take advantage of it now. One of the things the Government did was to allow small companies to go to investors and say: "You can get a tax break if you invest in our company". I think the play will be biased more towards the large multinationals and I am not sure that 1 want to put myself in the hands of those large multinationals, because I feel I would be more vulnerable. I would rather be dependent on a smaller Canadian company which takes its fate in its hands and its Canadian dollars and tries to do the job.
The difficulty I see in the change of policy is that it will skew and bias exploration and development away from small Canadian companies towards large multinationals.

speechtext:

The Government has to be sure that its plans to deal with non-monetary aspects of redress are also acceptable to the National Association of Japanese Canadians. U.S.S.R. PROPOSAL TO REDUCE NUCLEAR ARMAMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians, including those in a grade nine class in Virden, Manitoba, with whom I recently met, fervently desire the preservation of world peace. As a result, we applaud any serious proposal, irrespective of its origin, which might lead to fully verifiable nuclear disarmament.
While many Canadians, myself included, believe that the credibility of General Secretary Gorbachev's recent proposal for a nuclear-free world by the year 2000 would be substantially enhanced by an immediate decision to withdraw Soviet invasion forces from Afghanistan, the Gorbachev initiative still deserves serious consideration. Consequently, I and other Canadians welcomed the positive and thoughtful statement which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) made in response to the Gorbachev proposal last Thursday. Now, however, I urge both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to capitalize upon Canada's significantly improved relationship with the United States to ensure that American officials explore thoroughly this and any other proposal which may lead to fully verifiable nuclear disarmament.
Soviet officials must also be reminded of the need to address the substantial imbalance in conventional arms which is in the Soviet's favour, as that imbalance has led to the establishment of the western European-based nuclear forces as a deterrent. The fear and distrust which have prevailed since the cold war have let to a rapidly escalating arms race. If, as we hope, there is now a mutual will on the part of all world powers to de-escalate that arms race, much of the fear and distrust will disappear.

subtopic: TIME LIMITED ON SPEECHES AT THIRD READING-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
TIME LIMITED ON SPEECHES AT THIRD READING-RULING OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
I should like now to give a ruling with regard to a matter raised by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) on Friday, January 24, 1986. The Member for Ottawa-Vanier asked for clarification on the interpretation of Standing Order 36(1) in relation to the length of speeches at third reading. Having considered the matter and verifying

precedents I am now prepared to rule. Standing Order 36(1) reads as follows:
Unless otherwise provided in these Standing Orders, when the Speaker is in the Chair, no Member, except the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, or a Minister moving a government order and the Member speaking in reply immediately after such Minister, shall speak for more than twenty minutes at a time in any debate.
In situations where a Minister moves the motion for third reading and speaks first it is quite clear that the Opposition Member replying immediately after the Minister would be entitled to unlimited time. It would appear logical to me to carry this practice further and say that in those instances where the Minister's Parliamentary Secretary makes the first speech on behalf of the Government, he or she should have unlimited time and the Opposition Member replying immediately thereafter should also be entitled to unlimited time.
